summary: Ghost in the Pulse is a web app for monitoring astronaut health on deep-space missions, where Earth can be minutes away. It has three consoles: the astronaut on board, Mission Control on Earth (with a realistic signal delay), and an admin and flight surgeon console. Instead of one health score, it gives three outputs: physical status, well-being from a 30-second daily check-in, and open findings. It compares every reading with the astronaut’s own baseline, and a “ghost” forecast catches small drifts early. Missing data is never shown as healthy. An anatomical 3D body shows each organ system in its live status. A cardiovascular module watches for heart emergencies (ventricular tachycardia, ST elevation, low blood pressure) and tracks long-term risk factors. When a finding is urgent, the whole screen turns red, and 38 step-by-step protocols guide the crew without Earth. Each protocol can be read aloud. Crew can report symptoms and injuries, ask an onboard medical assistant in English or Arabic, and print a medical report. All data is simulated.
details:
GHOST IN THE PULSE — PROJECT DOCUMENTATION

NASA Space Apps Challenge · Astronaut health monitoring challenge

Team Ghost in the Pulse · Jordan University of Science and Technology (JUST)

DEMO LOGIN PINs

Admin ................................ 0000

Astronaut (demo astronaut TESTNAME) .. 1111

Mission Control (Ground) ............. 2222

========================================================================

1. OVERVIEW

========================================================================

Ghost in the Pulse is a web app that monitors astronaut health on deep-space missions, where help from Earth is minutes away. It watches each crew member against their own normal, warns early, and guides the crew step by step without waiting for Earth. It was built by team Ghost in the Pulse (Jordan University of Science and Technology) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, astronaut health monitoring challenge.

Tagline: Hearing what the body whispers before it screams.

The problem. On the way to Mars a radio message takes 3 to 22 minutes each way. A health problem can become an emergency before Mission Control even sees the first sign. Crews need a system that notices early, explains what it sees, and tells them what to do on board.

What we built.

- Three consoles, one crew, two time frames. The astronaut sees everything in real time; Mission Control sees the same data after a realistic signal delay; an admin and flight-surgeon console sets up the mission and runs demo scenarios.

- Three outputs, not one score. Physical status, well-being and open findings are shown separately, so a good mood never hides a bad heart rhythm.

- Early warning. Every reading is compared with the astronaut's own baseline, and a dashed "ghost" forecast runs just ahead of the live heart trace.

- Honest data. Missing or faulty data is never shown as healthy.

- Guidance that works without Earth. 38 step-by-step protocols, each readable aloud, an onboard medical assistant in English and Arabic, and SOS.

- Heart focus. A Cardiovascular Health Risk Intelligence module with a short-term emergency watch and a long-term risk profile.

- An anatomical 3D body that shows every organ system in its live status colour.

Status. A working prototype. All vitals, cabin readings, the signal delay and SOS are simulated; it is decision support for a hackathon, not a medical device and not an official NASA product.

========================================================================

2. THE THREE CONSOLES AND A DEMO RUN

========================================================================

One crew is seen through three windows: on board in real time, on Earth through the light-time delay, and from the flight surgeon's setup desk. All three run on the same shared state, so an action in one appears in the others.

| Console | Page | Who | Sees time as | Login |

| Astronaut | astronaut.html | One crew member, possibly gloved and stressed | Real time on board | Pick your name, then your 4-digit PIN (demo: TESTNAME, 1111) |

| Mission Control | ground.html | Flight controllers at a ground station | Delayed by the one-way light time | Pick a station, PIN 2222 |

| Admin and flight surgeon | admin.html | Mission setup, medical profile, demo control | Real time | PIN 0000 |

The landing page (index.html) explains the idea with a live pulse line and its ghost, shows the active mission (name, mission day, crew aboard, one-way delay, crew status) and lets each person choose a console.

Ground stations. Houston MCC, ESA ESOC Darmstadt, EAC Cologne (Earth), Gateway Station (lunar orbit) and ISS Hub (low Earth orbit). A closer station gets a shorter delay: Gateway sees a Moon crew almost live, the ISS Hub sees an ISS crew live.

Demo run (about 3 minutes).

1. Admin (PIN 0000): choose the mission profile (for example Mars Transit) and add a crew member with a PIN; set the one-way delay to "20 s (demo)" so judges see the delay without waiting.

2. Open the Astronaut console (TESTNAME, PIN 1111) in a second window and Mission Control (PIN 2222) in a third.

3. Admin > Scenarios: start one (for example "Heart Attack Signs (ST elevation)").

4. On board, the ECG ghost bends first, then an Urgent finding turns the whole page red; the guidance opens and can be read aloud.

5. Mission Control sees nothing until the signal arrives, then its Heart tab shows the emergency and every packet is visible in "Signal in transit".

6. Acknowledge, message the crew (the message also travels with the delay), stop the scenario, and print the medical report.

========================================================================

3. FEATURE REFERENCE

========================================================================

Every feature below is in the running prototype.

ASTRONAUT CONSOLE

Built for a busy, possibly gloved and stressed astronaut: 4 tabs, targets of 56 px or more, large numbers, one obvious action at a time.

- Top bar: mission elapsed time (MET), one-way delay, "Simulated" badge, theme switch, a notifications bell (count and colour of the worst open finding) and SOS.

- Status tab, always shown: a headline in plain words ("You're doing well, Omar." / "Emergency. Follow the steps."), the one next action, the three outputs (Physical status, Well-being, Findings), and four main readings: heart rate, blood oxygen, blood pressure, core temperature. Each reading shows its normal band, "your usual" range and its trend; tapping it opens its chart.

- Status tab, "Show more": the live ECG with its ghost forecast, four more readings (blood glucose, breathing rate, HRV, stress index), the 3D body, radiation dose (today, mission, career against the 600 mSv limit) and the cabin or suit air (oxygen, CO2, temperature, pressure). Anything hidden there that needs a look is lifted into "Also needs a look" next to the main readings, so a warning is never hidden.

- Report a problem: symptoms (12) and injuries (9 types), each opening the right guidance at once; plus a library of all 38 protocols.

- Tasks tab: daily check-in (30 seconds: mood, sleep, stress, tiredness, symptoms), a 10-tap reaction test (PVT-B settings), exercise log; weekly tasks (body mass, vision grid self-check, private medical conference); monthly tasks (cycle fitness test, hearing check, blood and urine samples); manual readings by hand (oximeter, pulse count, cuff, thermometer, finger-stick glucose, breathing count, NT-proBNP).

- Alerts (from the bell): every finding with its tier, the evidence behind it ("Why this alert?"), Open guidance, Acknowledge and Resolve.

- Messages tab: text with the ground; each message shows Saving, In transit, Delivered and Read, and arrives after the delay.

- Assist tab: a medical assistant that answers in English or Arabic from the onboard protocols and a cited knowledge base, on-device or through a cloud model.

- SOS: press and hold, sends an Urgent alert to the crew and Earth (simulated).

- Medical report: a printable report (10 sections) of status, vitals, check-ins, tests, manual readings, exercise, radiation, tasks and heart.

MISSION CONTROL CONSOLE

- Signal in transit: every packet of telemetry, alerts and messages drawn crossing between Earth and the spacecraft, with one-way time, round trip and distance.

- Crew cards: one per astronaut with the five hazard letters R I D G E coloured by status, heart rate, SpO2, temperature and "telemetry as of" age.

- Drill-down tabs per astronaut: Overview, Heart (short-term watch, long-term risk, reported symptoms and injuries), Body 3D, Charts (20 charts over 1 h, 24 h or 7 days, with hover values and a table view), and one tab per hazard (Radiation, Isolation, Distance, Gravity, Environment).

- Alerts received: filter by open or all and by severity; acknowledge; the crew's actions from the guidance (for example "I'm in the storm shelter").

- Comms: message one astronaut or the whole crew; send an advisory with a chosen protocol; both travel with the delay.

- Shared cabin panel and the same printable medical report.

ADMIN AND FLIGHT SURGEON CONSOLE

- Mission clock and link: mission profile (ISS, Moon, Mars transit, Mars surface), mission name and day, one-way delay (physical, or 0 s, 1.3 s, 20 s demo, 4, 12, 24 min, custom) and simulation speed.

- Crew roster: add, edit, remove and reactivate astronauts (name, callsign, role, agency, country, age, sex, PIN, prior career dose, optional baselines) and each one's heart risk profile.

- Demo scenarios: 11 scenarios started on one astronaut or the whole crew, stopped at any time.

- Thresholds view, console PINs and sound, AI settings (onboard model choice, cloud provider and key), data mode (local or cloud), export JSON, reset everything, and the alert audit log.

========================================================================

4. HEALTH ENGINE

========================================================================

The engine checks data quality first, compares each reading with the person's own baseline, and only then raises a finding with its evidence and the protocol to follow. It is decision support, never a diagnosis.

Three outputs, never one score.

- Physical status from sensor vitals: Stable, Data incomplete, Attention, Medical review or Urgent, with "10 of 10 readings valid" and "compared with your own baseline".

- Well-being from the 30-second daily check-in (0 to 100); after 30 hours without one it shows "Not current".

- Findings: the open alerts, counted by tier.

Data quality, before interpretation. Each channel is Valid, Missing, Stale, Suspected sensor error (implausible, flat-line, spike or contradictory), Re-measure (a safety-critical value checked again before it is trusted) or Not interpretable (HRV and stress during an irregular rhythm). Missing, stale, faulty and not-interpretable data are never counted as normal. A recent manual reading (for example a finger oximeter) is used when the sensor is off.

Personal baseline. Each astronaut's normal comes from resting, scenario-free readings at the same time of day on 14 pre-flight days (median and 1.4826 × MAD). It stays fixed in flight, so slow drift stays visible.

- one reading with |z| of 3 or more → "Unusual reading, measure again";

- |z| of 2 or more in 3 of the last 5 samples → "Unusual compared with your baseline";

- an EWMA (λ = 0.2) of z over 20 minutes crossing its control limit → "Trend forming": the ghost signal. It shows only after 2 minutes sustained and holds for at least 3 minutes, so it never flickers.

Population bands. Every vital also has normal, caution, warning and emergency bands from clinical norms and NASA-STD-3001 (for example heart rate normal 50–100 bpm, SpO2 normal 95% or more, CO2 limit 3 mmHg on the ISS).

Alert tiers.

| Tier (code) | Shown as | Meaning | Example |

| info | Informational | Note only | Daily check-in overdue |

| caution | Routine follow-up | Watch, repeat, log | Heart rate higher than your usual, still in the normal band |

| warning | Medical review | The flight surgeon should review | NT-proBNP 620 pg/mL |

| emergency | Urgent | Act now; page turns red | ST elevation, ventricular tachycardia, CO2 8.5 mmHg |

Alert lifecycle. A condition must last (for example 30 seconds for a vital, 10 seconds for a rhythm) before it raises. An alert only escalates, never quietly downgrades. Each side acknowledges separately; the other side learns after the delay. A sensor-driven alert resolves when the reading recovers; SOS, ground advisories and crew reports are closed by a person. A problem that returns after its alert closed opens a new alert (with a 1-minute guard against flapping).

Multi-symptom patterns. Findings that join exposures, risk factors, body changes and symptoms: headache with high CO2, vision change (SANS), space motion sickness, dizziness, nausea, fatigue, low mood, signs of hypoxia, and palpitations with an irregular rhythm.

Every finding explains itself. "Why this alert?" lists the evidence by type (sensor value, baseline, symptom, data quality, exposure) and the source in the knowledge base.

========================================================================

5. CARDIOVASCULAR HEALTH RISK INTELLIGENCE

========================================================================

The heart module watches one organ in two time frames: a short-term emergency watch that reacts in seconds, and a long-term risk profile the flight surgeon keeps. It lives in js/core/cardio.js and shows in Mission Control's Heart tab, the medical report and the ECG card.

Short term: emergency watch.

| Sign | Source | Urgent when | Medical review when |

| Rhythm (VT watch) | Live ECG | Ventricular tachycardia | Atrial fibrillation |

| ST segment | ECG, simulated lead II | Elevation of 1 mm or more | Depression of 1 mm or more |

| Blood pressure | Cuff | Systolic under 80 mmHg | Systolic under 90 mmHg |

| Heart rate, blood oxygen | ECG, oximeter | By their emergency bands | By their warning bands |

| NT-proBNP (heart strain) | Blood test entered by hand | — | 450 pg/mL or more (125–449 = follow-up) |

| Heart symptoms (24 h) | Crew report | Fainting; heart-type pain 4/10+ or with breathlessness, vomiting or dizziness | Milder chest-area pain; palpitations with dizziness |

ST elevation, or heart-type pain with low blood pressure, makes the watch Urgent on its own. The ECG chip then reads "ST elevation 2.8 mm" instead of "Regular rhythm", so a regular rhythm never shows green while the trace shows a heart-attack sign. A real ST reading needs a 12-lead ECG; ours is drawn on a simulated lead II and labelled so.

Long term: risk profile. Entered by the flight surgeon in the admin crew editor: height and weight (BMI, with weight replaced by the weekly body-mass task), LDL, HDL, triglycerides, smoking, high blood pressure, diabetes, known heart disease, kidney disease, past heart procedure, family history of early heart disease, and free-text medical, surgical and family history. The output is a list of recognised risk factors in the NCEP ATP III style (high HDL cancels one; age counts) and a level: Lower, Some or Higher risk.

- No % score on purpose. Framingham and the pooled cohort equations are not validated for astronauts, so a percentage would be invented.

- Blanks are never "low risk". Missing values show "Not entered" or "Incomplete".

- Private. The profile is seen by ground and the flight surgeon, not on the astronaut's screen, and is never sent to the AI assistant.

Demo scenarios. "Heart Attack Signs (ST elevation)" (ST +2.8 mm, faster pulse, falling blood pressure, lower oxygen) and "Ventricular Tachycardia" (about 175 bpm, wide complexes, low blood pressure). Each opens its own protocol: Possible heart attack, or Ventricular tachycardia (pulse check, CPR anchored in weightlessness, AED).

========================================================================

6. GUIDANCE, REPORTS AND THE ONBOARD ASSISTANT

========================================================================

The crew gets help without Earth in three ways: 38 step-by-step protocols, a "Report a problem" screen that opens the right one, and a medical assistant in English or Arabic.

Protocols. One step per screen in huge type, Back and Next, timers where a step takes time ("press for 10 minutes"), action buttons (do the check-in, message the ground, log a crew action, SOS), and at the end the signs that mean "press SOS or call the flight surgeon". Every protocol says whether it works without Earth, and is adapted for weightlessness (blood and vomit float, no running water, anchor yourself for CPR or abdominal thrusts). Medicines are always "as the onboard checklist says".

Read aloud. A button on every protocol reads the title, summary and each step as the crew moves through it, and says "Time is up" when a timer ends; the choice is remembered. Mission Control's checklist view reads the whole protocol. It uses the browser's built-in speech (Web Speech API): no key, no internet where the device has voices.

| Group | Protocol | Tier | Steps |

| Heart | Possible heart attack | Urgent | 7 |

| Heart | Ventricular tachycardia | Urgent | 6 |

| Heart | Irregular heart rhythm | Medical review | 8 |

| Heart | Fainting or feeling faint | Medical review | 6 |

| Heart | Chest pain | Medical review | 4 |

| Heart | Heart rate or blood pressure out of range | Routine follow-up | 5 |

| Injury | Cut or wound | Routine follow-up | 6 |

| Injury | Possible broken bone | Medical review | 6 |

| Injury | Burn | Routine follow-up | 6 |

| Injury | Head injury | Medical review | 7 |

| Injury | Something in the eye or eye injury | Routine follow-up | 6 |

| Injury | Nosebleed | Routine follow-up | 6 |

| Injury | Sprain, strain or dislocation | Routine follow-up | 6 |

| Injury | Chemical or toxic exposure | Medical review | 6 |

| Injury | Electric shock | Medical review | 6 |

| Crewmate emergency | Choking | Urgent | 6 |

| Crewmate emergency | Seizure (fit) | Urgent | 7 |

| Crewmate emergency | Allergic reaction | Medical review | 6 |

| Crewmate emergency | SOS: medical emergency | Urgent | 7 |

| Symptom | Short of breath | Medical review | 5 |

| Symptom | Headache | Routine follow-up | 5 |

| Symptom | Motion sickness and vomiting | Routine follow-up | 6 |

| Symptom | Belly pain | Medical review | 6 |

| Symptom | Back pain | Routine follow-up | 5 |

| Symptom | Cannot pass urine | Medical review | 6 |

| Symptom | Tooth pain or broken tooth | Routine follow-up | 5 |

| Symptom | Signs of infection | Routine follow-up | 6 |

| Radiation | Solar storm: go to shelter | Medical review | 7 |

The tier column is each protocol's default; a finding can raise it (for example a head injury with fainting is Urgent).

Report a problem. 12 symptoms (pain or dull ache with place and a 0–10 slider, short of breath, dizzy, fainted, palpitations, nausea or vomiting, headache, allergic reaction, cannot pass urine, tooth pain, signs of infection with place) and 9 injury types, each with one to three yes/no danger-sign questions. The report is saved on board, raises the right tier, opens the matching protocol at once, and reaches Earth after the delay.

Onboard medical assistant. Answers in English or Arabic, grounded in the open alerts, the onboard protocols and a cited knowledge base of 28 entries (NASA, CSA and research sources). Three ways to run it:

- On the device, no internet: an open-weight model in the browser with WebLLM (WebGPU): Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen2.5 1.5B (default) or Qwen2.5 3B.

- Cloud, optional: Groq (gpt-oss-120b), Google Gemini, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with the team's own key.

- No model at all: a rule-based answer that matches the question (English or Arabic words) to the right protocols and knowledge entries.

Only the callsign and role leave the device, never the name, age, sex or heart profile. Serious signs always point to the protocol and SOS.

========================================================================

7. ANATOMICAL 3D BODY

========================================================================

An interactive human body shows where in the body each problem is, with every organ system coloured by its live status. It is built with three.js (WebGL) and appears on the astronaut's Status tab (under "Show more") and in Mission Control's Body 3D tab, where it runs at the delayed ground time.

- A real human model. The skin is the MakeHuman base mesh (13,380 vertices, 26,756 triangles) with a young male, muscular shape applied, in the standard A-pose. It is released by its authors as CC0 (public domain) and stored offline in the project.

- Inside it: brain (two hemispheres, cerebellum, brainstem, spinal cord), eyes with optic nerves, heart (chambers, atria, aorta, pulmonary artery, coronary arteries) that beats at the live heart rate, lungs (three lobes right, two left) with trachea and bronchi that breathe at the live breathing rate, stomach, liver, pancreas, small and large intestine, kidneys, and the main arteries and veins to the head, arms and legs.

- Skeleton: skull and jaw, 26 vertebrae, 12 curved rib pairs (7 reach the breastbone, 3 join the cartilage, 2 float), sternum, shoulder blades, pelvis, and paired forearm and shin bones, hand and foot bones. Arm and leg bones follow the model's own joint positions.

- Layers: Skin, Organs, Vessels and Skeleton can be shown or hidden. Skin alone draws a solid, lit body; with anything inside shown, the skin turns to see-through glass.

- Eight systems with pins: Brain and mind, Eyes (SANS), Heart and circulation, Lungs and airway, Stomach and blood sugar, Bones and muscles, Skin and temperature, Whole-body radiation (a particle field that speeds up in a solar storm). Tap a pin or an organ to see every reading behind it, its data quality, its alerts and the protocols to open.

- Status colours: green (nominal), dashed purple (ghost signal), amber (caution), orange (warning), flashing red (urgent), wireframe (no data). Missing data is shown as "No data", never green.

- Works everywhere: drag, pinch or arrow keys to turn; reduced motion stops the animation; without WebGL a list of the eight systems replaces the 3D view.

========================================================================

8. SIMULATION: READINGS, MISSIONS, SCENARIOS AND DELAY

========================================================================

All telemetry is simulated deterministically: each value is a pure function of the astronaut, the mission time, the mission profile and the running scenarios, with seeded noise. Every open window computes the same numbers without sending raw telemetry, and Mission Control simply reads them at "now minus the one-way delay".

17 channels. Bands are demo values from clinical norms and NASA-STD-3001, simplified for a simulation.

| Channel | Unit | Normal | Warning limit |

| Heart rate | bpm | 50–100 | 40–150 |

| Blood oxygen (SpO2) | % | 95 or more | 88 or more |

| Blood pressure, systolic | mmHg | 90–135 | 80–180 |

| Blood pressure, diastolic | mmHg | 55–85 | 45–110 |

| Core temperature | °C | 36.0–37.9 | 35.0–39.5 |

| Blood glucose | mg/dL | 70–140 | 54–250 |

| Breathing rate | br/min | 10–20 | 6–30 |

| Heart rate variability (RMSSD) | ms | 19 or more | 10 or more |

| Stress index (simulated) | 0–100 | 50 or less | 85 or less |

| Radiation dose rate | µSv/h | 100 or less | 1000 or less |

| Bone loss rate (projected) | %/month | 0.8 or less | 2.0 or less |

| Oxygen partial pressure | kPa | 19.5–23.5 | 14.0–30.0 |

| Carbon dioxide | mmHg | 3.0 or less | 7.6 or less |

| Cabin temperature | °C | 20–25 | 15–32 |

| Humidity | %RH | 30–60 | 15–85 |

| Cabin pressure | kPa | 97–103 | 70–105 |

| Noise | dBA | 65 or less | 85 or less |

The ECG is synthesised beat by beat (P, Q, R, S and T waves) from the live heart rate, with four rhythms (sinus, extra beats, atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia) and an ST shift. Glucose rises after meals at 07:00, 13:00 and 19:00.

Four mission profiles.

| Profile | Gravity | One-way delay | Cosmic-ray dose |

| ISS, low Earth orbit | 0 g | about 0 s | about 0.5 mSv/day |

| Artemis, lunar surface | 0.166 g | 1.3 s | 1.37 mSv/day |

| Mars transit | 0 g | 3.1–22.4 min, varying with the planets' positions | 1.8 mSv/day |

| Mars surface | 0.38 g | 3.1–22.4 min, plus a 2-week solar-conjunction blackout | 0.67 mSv/day |

The admin can override the delay (0 s, 1.3 s, 20 s demo, 4, 12 or 24 min, or custom). Delays are real seconds and do not speed up with the simulation speed.

11 demo scenarios. Solar particle event, CO2 buildup, hypoxia from a suit or module leak, fatigue and isolation, low blood sugar after a spacewalk, cardiac arrhythmia (Mars), heart attack signs (ST elevation), ventricular tachycardia, pulse oximeter fault, chest strap off (no signal), and bone loss from missed exercise. Each has an onset, hold and decay; some can be eased by a crew action from the guidance ("I'm in the storm shelter", "Backup CO2 scrubbing is on", "I took 15 g of fast sugar"). The two sensor faults show that the system tells a broken sensor from a sick astronaut.

========================================================================

9. TECHNOLOGY

========================================================================

A static web app with no framework and no build step: it runs from any static host (we use Firebase Hosting) or straight from the files over file://, and works offline.

Languages.

| Language | Used for | Size |

| JavaScript (plain, classic scripts, one GITP namespace) | Simulation, health engine, alerts, heart module, UI, 3D body, assistant | about 12,500 lines in 53 files (not counting libraries and data assets) |

| HTML5 | 4 pages (landing, astronaut, Mission Control, admin) and a style guide | about 1,270 lines |

| CSS3 (custom properties, container queries, light and dark themes) | All styling | about 2,600 lines in 10 files |

| GLSL | The see-through "glass" and solid skin shader of the 3D body | 1 shader |

| Firestore Security Rules | Validating every document written to the cloud | 1 file |

| Python | 70 automated browser test scripts (Playwright), building the 3D body mesh, rendering the promo video | test and build tooling only |

Libraries and browser APIs.

| Library or API | Version | Why | Loaded |

| three.js | r159 | 3D body (WebGL) | Bundled in the project |

| Firebase JS SDK (compat) | 10.12.2 | Optional cloud sync with Firestore | From gstatic.com, only if configured |

| WebLLM (MLC) | 0.2.88 | Optional onboard AI model in the browser (WebGPU) | From jsDelivr, only when chosen |

| Web Speech API | built in | Read aloud | Browser |

| Canvas 2D, SVG | built in | ECG strip, charts, sparklines, signal in transit | Browser |

| localStorage, BroadcastChannel | built in | Local data and live sync between windows | Browser |

No analytics, no trackers, no other third-party code.

Code layout. js/data/ (missions, hazards, vitals, scenarios, protocols, rules, knowledge base, body mesh), js/core/ (store and adapters, clock, simulation, ECG, data quality, baseline, patterns, health, heart module, alerts, comms, auth, assistant, boot), js/components/ (mission bar, vital tiles, ECG line, charts, trend chart, 3D body, protocol viewer, report, signal in transit) and js/pages/ (one script per page).

Data and storage. Only state is stored, never raw telemetry: mission settings, crew, scenarios, check-ins, reaction tests, exercise, alerts, messages, manual readings, weekly and monthly tasks, crew reports and the audit log. Two adapters share one interface:

- Local: localStorage, with storage events and BroadcastChannel so an action in one window appears in the others at once.

- Cloud (optional): Cloud Firestore under one demo path, with real-time listeners. If it fails to load or connect, the app falls back to local mode by itself, and a failed write is shown as "not saved", never silently lost.

Security (demo grade). 4-digit PINs per role, with a lockout after repeated failures. Firestore rules allow only known collections, check each document's shape and size, and close the database on 1 March 2027. The optional cloud-AI key lives in js/config/ai-config.js or is entered in the admin console; in a public deployment it is readable by visitors, so we use a free-tier key that is rotated after the event, and a server-side proxy is the planned fix. Real Anonymous Auth with role checks is the documented next step.

========================================================================

10. DESIGN AND ACCESSIBILITY

========================================================================

The look follows NASA's "Flight Data File": the plain, ruled checklists astronauts actually fly with, readable under stress.

- Palette: NASA blue ink on white by day; deep-space navy at night; NASA red kept for one job, the live point of the pulse. No NASA logo or insignia is used.

- Signature motif: the live ECG on strip-chart paper with its dashed ghost running ahead, and the five RIDGE hazard letters.

- Type: Archivo (one family, condensed for headings) and Martian Mono only for the mission clock; numbers use tabular figures. Both fonts are self-hosted so the app works offline.

- Panels: heavy 2 px top rules and code tabs (R-01, COMM, P-CARD-ACS), like procedure IDs on a checklist card.

- Status is never colour alone: every status has a colour, a shape (circle, triangle, diamond, octagon, dashed ring, slashed circle) and a word.

- Urgent alarm: the whole page turns red with diagonal stripes and an alarm bar until someone on that side acknowledges; Mission Control's alarm starts only when the signal arrives.

Accessibility.

- WCAG AA contrast checked automatically in light and dark themes, on desktop (1280 px) and phone (390 px) widths.

- Glove-friendly targets: 56 px minimum on the astronaut console, 72 px for primary actions; 44 px elsewhere.

- Visible keyboard focus everywhere; arrow keys, Home and End move between tabs; the 3D body turns with arrow keys; dialogs trap focus and Escape closes them.

- Reduced-motion users get still frames (ECG, 3D body, alarm without flashing).

- Screen-reader labels on controls and live regions for toasts and alerts; the guidance can be read aloud.

- Works from 320 px phones to wide control-room screens; on phones the tabs become a bottom bar.

========================================================================

11. TESTING AND QUALITY

========================================================================

The app is tested in a real browser (Chromium, driven by Playwright) by about 70 automated scripts that click through the consoles the way a judge would and check the results.

| Area | What the tests check |

| End to end | Admin adds crew and starts scenarios; the astronaut and Mission Control react; acknowledgements and messages cross the delay |

| Health engine | Alert tiers, escalation, re-opening, the ghost signal not flickering, baselines, patterns, sensor faults versus real illness, manual readings |

| Heart module | Long-term risk levels, "Not entered" for blanks, ST elevation and VT alarms, NT-proBNP, crew reports at the right tier, Mission Control's Heart tab at ground time |

| Guidance | All 38 protocols open and run to the last step; read aloud speaks every step and stops when closed; 9 injuries and 12 symptoms open the right protocol |

| 3D body | Layers, pins not covered by other organs, light and dark themes, phone layout |

| Charts and tasks | 20 charts with hover values and table view; weekly and monthly task states and findings |

| Cloud | Firestore mode, offline fallback, failed writes shown as "not saved" |

| Accessibility and layout | Colour contrast in both themes, no text cut off, no horizontal overflow at 320, 390 and 1280 px |

| Long run | A soak test that runs the simulation for a long period without errors |

Every change is re-run against the suite, and no browser console errors are allowed.

12. SAFETY, PRIVACY AND LIMITATIONS

========================================================================

We designed the prototype to be honest about what it knows and what it does not.

Honesty rules built into the product.

- Every screen that shows vitals carries a "Simulated" badge; SOS is labelled as simulated; no value is presented as a real astronaut measurement.

- Missing, stale or faulty data is never shown as healthy, and a broken sensor is told apart from a sick astronaut.

- No single health score, and no invented percentages (no fake heart-risk %).

- Findings show their evidence and source; nothing is called a diagnosis.

- Protocols are first-aid level and send medicine decisions to the onboard checklist and the flight surgeon.

- No external service is shown as connected when it is not.

Privacy. Only the callsign and role are ever sent to an AI model, never the name, age, sex or heart profile. The heart profile and medical history are visible to Mission Control and the flight surgeon only. In local mode nothing leaves the browser.

Limitations.

- All data is simulated; no real wearable is connected yet (the design follows CSA's Bio-Monitor style of shirt-based sensors).

- ST-segment and VT detection run on a simulated single lead; a real system needs a 12-lead ECG and validated algorithms.

- Thresholds are simplified demo values, not flight rules, and have not been reviewed by a flight surgeon.

- Login is demo-grade (PINs); real authentication, role checks and a server-side AI proxy are the next steps.

- The onboard AI model needs a WebGPU-capable browser and a one-time download of about 0.9 to 2.5 GB.

- Read aloud uses the device's voices; protocols are in English (the assistant answers in Arabic too).

Next steps. Connect a real wearable stream, validate thresholds with clinicians, add Arabic protocol text, real authentication with Firebase Anonymous Auth and role checks, and a proxy for the cloud-AI key.

14. HOW TO RUN IT, CREDITS AND LICENCES

========================================================================

Try it in three minutes.

1. Open the live site, or open index.html from the project folder (no install needed).

2. Admin (PIN 0000): pick a mission profile, set the delay to "20 s demo", add or check the crew, and start a scenario such as "Heart attack signs".

3. Astronaut (demo astronaut TESTNAME, PIN 1111): see the alert at once, follow the protocol step by step, use read aloud, or tap "Report a problem".

4. Mission Control (PIN 2222): watch the signal travel, then see the same event arrive 20 seconds later, with the Heart tab, 3D body, charts and report.

Open the consoles in separate windows or devices side by side to see the delay.

Demo PINs: Admin 0000 · Astronaut TESTNAME 1111 · Mission Control (Ground) 2222

Deploy. firebase deploy publishes the public/ folder to Firebase Hosting. To share data across devices, fill js/config/firebase-config.js with a Firebase project's web config and deploy firestore.rules; without it, the app runs in local mode in each browser.
